sections.content: If you're wholesaling real estate, one question comes up on every single deal: how much should I charge as my assignment fee? Charge too little and you're leaving thousands of dollars behind. Charge too much and your buyer walks away. Getting this number right is one of the most important skills a wholesaler can develop. An assignment fee calculator for wholesale deals takes the guesswork out of this process and helps you structure offers that work for everyone at the table.
What Is an Assignment Fee in Wholesale Real Estate?

When you wholesale a property, you don't actually buy it. Instead, you get it under contract with a seller, then assign that contract to an end buyer — usually a cash investor or a house flipper — for a fee. That fee is your assignment fee. It's your profit for finding the deal, negotiating the price, and connecting the seller to a buyer. Assignment fees typically range from $5,000 to $20,000 on a standard residential deal, though experienced wholesalers in hot markets regularly earn $25,000 or more per transaction.
Your assignment fee isn't a guess — it's a math problem. When you understand the numbers, you can confidently negotiate both sides of the deal.
The Core Formula: How to Calculate Your Assignment Fee

The assignment fee is the difference between what you locked the property up for and what your end buyer is willing to pay. Here's the simple formula: Assignment Fee = Buyer's Offer Price minus Your Contract Price. But to make this work, you need to know what your buyer will pay — and that starts with understanding After Repair Value (ARV) and the Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO).
Step 1: Calculate the ARV

ARV is what the property will be worth after it's been fully renovated. You find this by looking at comparable sales — recently sold homes in the same neighborhood with similar size, condition, and features. If a fully fixed-up 3-bedroom ranch in your target area sells for $250,000, that's your ARV benchmark. Tools like our free [Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) can help you plug in comps and get a reliable ARV fast, especially if you're just getting started.
Step 2: Calculate the Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO)

The MAO is the most your cash buyer can pay for the property and still make a profit. Most investors use the 70% rule as a baseline: MAO = (ARV x 70%) minus Repair Costs. Using our example, if ARV is $250,000 and estimated repairs are $40,000, the MAO would be: ($250,000 x 0.70) minus $40,000 = $175,000 minus $40,000 = $135,000. This means your buyer is willing to pay up to $135,000 for the deal.
Step 3: Build In Your Assignment Fee

Now that you know what your buyer will pay ($135,000), you need to get the property under contract for less. If you negotiate the seller down to $120,000, your assignment fee is $15,000. Here's how it looks: Contract Price with Seller = $120,000. Contract Price to Buyer = $135,000. Assignment Fee = $15,000. That $15,000 is your paycheck for putting the deal together. The key is locking up the property low enough that there's room for your fee without squeezing your buyer's margins.

Always work backwards from the buyer's MAO when making your offer to the seller. If the MAO is $135,000 and you want a $15,000 fee, your maximum contract price is $120,000. Never let your assignment fee eat into your buyer's profit — you'll lose the deal.

sections.content: Factors That Affect How Much You Can Charge

Not every deal supports the same assignment fee. Several factors influence how much room you have to work with. Understanding these will help you spot high-fee opportunities and avoid thin deals that aren't worth your time.

items: Seller Motivation: A highly motivated seller — facing foreclosure, divorce, or inherited property — is more likely to accept a lower price, giving you more margin.
Property Condition: The worse the condition, the lower the seller's expectations and the higher the repair budget, which can actually create more fee room if you buy right.
Buyer Demand in the Market: When cash buyers are hungry for inventory, they'll sometimes pay closer to full MAO, allowing you to capture more of the spread.
Deal Speed: A clean title, motivated seller, and fast close make your deal more valuable. Buyers pay a premium for deals that won't drag on.
Your Negotiation Skills: The better you are at negotiating with sellers, the more room you create between the contract price and the buyer's MAO.

sections.content: Common Mistakes Wholesalers Make With Assignment Fees

New wholesalers often make one of two errors: they set their fee too high and scare off buyers, or they don't factor in their fee at all when making offers and end up working for almost nothing. The most common mistake is padding the contract price up to the buyer's full MAO, leaving no room for your assignment fee. Another big error is forgetting to account for closing costs, holding costs, or title issues that can shrink the buyer's profit and make your deal less attractive. If you're just getting started, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) walks through how to structure your first deal from the ground up.

Shoot for an assignment fee that leaves your buyer at least 15-20% profit margin after repairs and closing costs. A buyer who makes good money on your deal will come back again and again — and referrals from happy cash buyers are worth their weight in gold.
How to Present Your Assignment Fee to Buyers

Transparency builds trust with buyers. Most experienced investors know you're making money — they just want to make sure the deal still works for them. Present your deals with clear numbers: the purchase price, estimated repair costs, ARV, and projected buyer profit. When your buyer can see they're walking into a deal with 20-25% margin after your fee, they won't push back on your $15,000 payday. For a deeper walkthrough of the entire process, the [How to Wholesale Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesale-real-estate-beginners-guide) covers how to build buyer relationships and present deals professionally.
The best wholesalers don't just find deals — they deliver certainty. When your buyer trusts your numbers, your assignment fee becomes a non-issue.
